abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can cause acute and persistent neurological manifestations, and evidence suggests these effects may be at least partly explained by direct effects of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike protein, which includes neuroinflammation, cognitive dysfunction, and persistent pain. Because the developing brain undergoes finely regulated processes of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and cerebrovascular maturation, exposure to SARS-CoV-2 or its components during this critical period may interfere with neurodevelopment. We therefore investigated whether neonatal exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein affects processes underlying brain development. To this end, we used a mouse model previously developed by our group, where Swiss mice received an injection (s.c.) of spike protein from the ancestral viral strain or vehicle at postnatal day 1 (P1). Body weight, body length, and the righting reflex were evaluated until postnatal day 20 (P20). At P10, mouse brains were analyzed for cell proliferation, neural cell populations, and cerebrovascular organization, while blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed at P20 using Evans Blue. Neonatal spike protein exposure did not affect body weight, body length, or postural righting reflex. At P10, cell proliferation in spike-exposed animals was comparable to control groups, whereas region-specific alterations in SOX2-positive cells and TBR1-positive neurons were observed. Spike protein exposure did not broadly alter cerebrovascular architecture or BBB permeability, although increased IB4 fluorescence was detected in the lateral dentate gyrus (DG). Our findings provide evidence that exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein during postnatal development can influence specific aspects of neural development, highlighting the importance of understanding how viral components may affect the developing brain during critical windows of vulnerability. Keywords: spike protein, brain development, coronavirus, COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, cerebrovasculature.
